Playbook:

- The escort payout (5 points each way, mutual) is the biggest scoring lever in the game — far larger than the 4 points for a hit. When the escort stage is put to me, I always name someone, never none.

- But do not keep naming a boat that never reciprocates. I named Foxtrot round after round after proposing mutual escort and Foxtrot never claimed me once — wasted escort stages. After one or two rounds of non-reciprocation, switch my escort claim to a different boat.

- Validate every name before submitting. In one round I claimed escort on "Delta" when the live boats were Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor — a nonexistent name, almost certainly a forfeited stage. Re-read the boat list each time; a wasted claim is as bad as none.

- If no one reciprocates at all (in my episode all boats just posted "steady on station" and nothing else), rotate my escort claims among the live shooters anyway — it costs nothing and keeps a chance of an accidental or late mutual match. Do not give up on the stage just because deals have failed.

- Keep trying to set up arrangements in notes even when boats are silent — but one cooperative proposal per boat; if a boat ignores it twice, stop asking and redirect. A plain "steady on station" note is a wasted stage; even in the last rounds I should have made one concrete offer ("whoever claims me this round, I claim them next") rather than nothing.

- The best reciprocator candidate may be the boat that keeps hitting me — a mutual escort claim pays us both 5 and gives them a reason to stop shooting me (a hit only pays them 4). Propose exactly that in a note: "stop firing on me, claim escort instead — 5 beats your 4."

- Track claims made and honored: reward boats that reciprocated by claiming them again, and drop boats that don't. Never break a working reciprocal arrangement for a shot at 4 points when 5+5 is on the table.

- Firing: vary the cell each round and use misses as information — aim at untried cells, note where incoming shots on me come from to guess habits. My varied misses suggest the targets randomize their hides; shooting is genuinely low-yield (6 rounds, 0 hits) and I shouldn't spend note-stage capital on it.

- Hiding: when one boat hits me, that is information — jump far away the next round (different end of the line, not an adjacent cell) and abandon any cells I've used before. Getting hit costs a point each time and compounds over the patrol.

- Claims about my own shots: always report the true result. Honesty cost nothing; lying risks contradiction in later notes for no clear gain.

- Firing on Harbor is a trap: 3 points once, but the stated penalty is removal from the patrol (and losing all escort income). Never fire on Harbor, even in the last round.

- Score arithmetic matters for placement: hits pay the shooter 4 and cost the target 1, so being shot is slow bleed (-1 per hit) while my misses earn nothing. With a -1 final score, my losses came entirely from taking hits — so defense (hiding unpredictably) and escort income outrank everything else. Never repeat a hiding cell across rounds if I can avoid it; rotate ends of the line.

- Overall priority when I sit down: first secure a standing mutual-escort arrangement with whichever boat answers notes cooperatively — and if nobody cooperates, keep rotating escort claims among live shooters anyway. Treat shooting as secondary income, hide unpredictably every round, and treat hits on me as the loudest alarm in the game.

PLAYBOOK — sonar picket, any role

**Hiding stage**
- Never reuse the same cell twice in a row; if I hid at n last round and survived, move at least 2 cells away. Hunters pattern-match on repeats.
- Against an opponent who has missed me repeatedly at mid cells, shift to an edge (1, 2, 8, 9). Mid cells (4–6) are where undisciplined shooters default. This worked twice now: I hid at 2 and 8, six rounds, never took a hit — Echo missed me every single round.
- If my hunter is likely to be eliminated or redirected soon, assume I become the next target and re-randomize rather than staying comfortable.
- Watch the hit/miss log for MY boat's hunter: repeated misses tell me which cells my hunter over-fires. That log is free intel.
- Keep hiding conservative even in the final round — a last-round hit still costs a point and I have no upside for risk.

**Firing stage**
- The standing order on target selection is a safe default; deviating only with solid intel on the target's pattern.
- But obedience on targets is not the problem — cell choice is. Across twelve shots (edges and center both) I never hit once. Neither "avoid center" nor "always center" is a rule. Instead: open center (5), and if the target survives, alternate systematically — the log shows my misses, so cover the cells I have NOT yet fired at that target. Never re-fire a cell at the same target after a miss.
- Track where hits land on other boats: Gamma hit Echo round after round, almost certainly by reading Echo's mid-cell habit. Copy what successful shooters do — if a target keeps getting hit by someone else, the hider is patterned; aim where the pattern says, before the target dies.
- Do not fire on Harbor. The 3-point payroll grab is not worth being put off the board for the rest of the patrol.

**Claim stage**
- Claim truthfully, always. The office already knows the truth; deception only muddies my own record of where hits landed.

**Escort stage**
- Never skip the escort claim. The 5-point mutual payout is the game's best scoring mechanism.
- Ask directly in my note ("Gamma, I'll cover you if you cover me"). Explicit offers are better than vague ones — but note that even explicit offers got zero reciprocation this patrol. The other boats may simply not be reading notes or not care.
- Do not stay loyal to a non-reciprocating partner. I named Echo for four rounds with no payout, then switched to Gamma for two — still nothing. New rule: name my first-choice partner in round 1, and if no reciprocation by end of round 2, alternate my claim between the other boats each round. A single lucky match pays 5; loyalty pays 0.
- Match my claim to whoever most recently hit someone or posted a substantive note — a boat actively engaged is more likely to be filing claims at all.
- Expect zero escort income as the baseline. Treat any payout as a bonus, not a plan.

**Overall scoring math**
- This patrol: Gamma won on hits alone; I finished 0 with no escort income despite asking explicitly. Hits, not escorts, decided it.
- Priority order: (1) don't get hit — this I do well, keep it; (2) actually land hits — this I have never done, treat it as my main weakness; (3) escort lottery tickets.
- Track points every round. If a rival is running up hits on a patterned hider, that hider's cell habit is visible in the log — exploit it before the target dies.
- Gamma's path to winning: find a boat that hides predictably and keep hitting it. My path: read the log for repeat-hit victims, cover my own unfired cells on my assigned target, and take cheap escort shots.

**What clearly did not work**
- Any fixed firing pattern: edge shots missed, center shots missed, six misses each mix. The fix is systematic coverage of unfired cells, not pattern loyalty.
- Escort loyalty to a non-reciprocating boat (Echo): zero payout. Even switching late and asking explicitly (Gamma): zero payout. Switch earlier, keep switching, expect nothing.
- What did work and keep: edge hiding (never hit in twelve rounds of being shot at), truthful claims, never skipping the escort claim itself, following the standing order on target selection.

2.text:
Playbook for next time:

- When the office privately tells me my shot result, I always claim exactly that. The claim must match the private result anyway, and truthfully claiming a hit scores the 4 points. This line worked every round; keep it.
- At the escort stage, I always name another live boat, never none — it costs nothing and a mutual claim pays 5. But do not count on it: I claimed Echo every round and it was never reciprocated. Treat escorts as a lottery ticket, not a scoring lever. Keep the standing claim to the same boat all game (consistency is the only way a pact could ever form), but build my plan around hits instead.
- Hits are my main scoring lever. Track which cells have hit which target and which have missed. When a cell hits, firing the SAME cell again next round is worth one try — targets sometimes don't move — but it is not guaranteed: I hit Echo at a cell in round 4, refired it in round 5 and missed. So after refiring a hit cell once and missing, rotate away immediately rather than grinding the same spot.
- After a miss, change cells. Edges and a spread pattern worked for hiding (standing-order shooters missed me all game while I varied edge cells like 2 and 9), and edge fire cells produced my one hit. Keep avoiding the middle and repeating cells when hiding.
- Correct my expectations on totals: in this episode I scored only one hit in six rounds for +4 total (with Echo at -1 from taking my hit). The pure hit strategy is still the best available, but it is thin — one hit in six rounds is a realistic outcome, so don't relax if I land an early hit; keep firing deliberately every round.
- Never fire on Harbor. The 3-point jetterson is tempting, but the standing signal threatens removal from the board for the rest of the patrol, forfeiting all future rounds. Not tested, and I don't intend to test it.
- Notes: everyone posting "steady on station" gave nothing, and pact-signaling notes got no response. Keep my note boring and consistent; read others' only for deviations from their usual wording. Don't spend effort coordinating through notes.
- If my shots keep missing late, don't panic-switch to other levers — there are none besides hits and the (unreliable) escort. Keep varying fire cells systematically and keep the escort claim running as a free side bet.
- Watch the points summary and the round-by-round shot log each hide stage: the history lines (who fired at whom, hit or miss) are the best information I get. Use them to deduce where a target is NOT hiding and to fire cells no one has eliminated yet. Six rounds is short — start varying fire cells from round 1 rather than settling into a comfortable pattern that only lands once.
